# Soṇa Sutta (Ud 5.6 (PTS Ud 57))

**ID:** Ud 5.6 (PTS Ud 57)
**Section:** Udāna (ud)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Soṇa Sutta* (Ud 5.6; PTS Ud 57) recounts the story of the monk Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa (or Kuṭikaṇṇa), a young man residing in the remote western region of Avanti who is only able to obtain higher ordination after protracted delays due to the scarcity of bhikkhus in the border country [SuttaCentral; Fronsdal 2016; Levman 2014]. Having trained under Mahā Kaccāna, Soṇa undertakes a journey to meet the Buddha and stays overnight in the Buddha's own dwelling [Fronsdal 2016; Levman 2014]. Towards dawn, invited by the Buddha to speak or recite the Dhamma, Soṇa chants all sixteen poems of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* (found in the *Sutta Nipāta*) with clear intonation and delivery, earning the Buddha's high praise and formal approval (*abbhanumodi*) [SuttaCentral; Fronsdal 2016; Levman 2014; Garfield and Westerhoff 2015; O'Neill 2016].

Scholars consider this discourse a crucial benchmark for the history and transmission of early Buddhist literature [Fronsdal 2016; Levman 2014]. It provides direct canonical testimony that the *Aṭṭhakavagga* already existed as an independent, organized sixteen-poem collection at an extremely early stage [Fronsdal 2016; Levman 2014]. The narrative also illustrates the reliance on memorized metric poetry for preserving and disseminating Buddhist doctrine, as well as the importance attached to proper chanting diction and phonetic fidelity [Fronsdal 2016; Levman 2014; Garfield and Westerhoff 2015]. Furthermore, the episode is studied as an early canonical precedent for internal cross-referencing and textual recitation within Buddhist scriptural traditions [Levman 2014; O'Neill 2016].

The sutta's narrative is closely mirrored in the Vinaya literature across multiple early Buddhist schools [Fronsdal 2016; Levman 2014]. Within the Pali canon, both SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus verify extensive shared text between Ud 5.6 and the *Cammakkhandhaka* (Kd 5 / Vin I 194–198), with DharmaNexus identifying 73 matching passages comprising over 17,000 characters [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Levman 2014; Garfield and Westerhoff 2015]. SuttaCentral also records passage parallels to verse sections in the *Udānavarga* (UV 28, UVS 28, Uv Kg 28) and Chinese translations (T 212 and T 213) [SuttaCentral]. In addition, DharmaNexus records substantial Pali-internal text reuse with texts such as *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* Pārājika 1 and the *Raṭṭhapāla Sutta* (MN 82), alongside cross-language alignments with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D0001), the *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99), and the *Madhyamāgama* (T 26) [DharmaNexus].

- Passage-level parallels (SuttaCentral): UV 28 Pāpavarga; T 212.29 ◎惡行品第二十九; T 213.28 法集要頌經罪障品第二十八; Uv Kg 28 Sin; UVS 28 Pāpavarga; Kd 5 Cammakkhandhaka
- Mentioned in (SuttaCentral): snp4.1-16
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Cammakkhandhaka (Kd 5) (§15.2–20.4 ↔ §13.8.2–13.10.7); Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pārājika 1 (Bu-Vb Pj1) (§2.2–3.1 ↔ §5.1.7–5.1.9); Raṭṭhapāla Sutta (MN 82 (PTS MN ii 54)) (§2.2–3.1 ↔ §4.3–5.1_0); Aṭṭhakanipāta (AN 8) (§3.1–4.1 ↔ §46.1.3_0–46.1.4); Dasakanipāta (AN 10) (§3.1–4.1 ↔ §26.1.2_0–26.1.3); Bhesajjakkhandhaka (Kd 6) (§11.1–12.1 ↔ §15.1.2–15.1.4); Mahākhandhaka (Kd 1) (§15.1–15.2 ↔ §31.4.2–31.4.5); Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16 (PTS DN ii 72)) (§13.4–14.1_0 ↔ §1.2.2–1.2.4)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): འདུལ་བ་གཞི། (vinayavastu) (D0001) [bo]; 雜阿含經 (ZH_T02_0099) [zh]; 中阿含經 (ZH_T01_0026) [zh]; 中阿含經 (ZH_T01_0026) [zh]
